name: Western shirts with pearl snaps

lead: A Western shirt has a decorative yoke across front and back, long sleeves, and often snap fasteners and pocket flaps. The pearl-snap version replaces buttons with snaps, giving a recognizable look from rodeo and singing-cowboy wardrobes.
It helps looks as a statement piece: the yoke visually widens the shoulders and the style signals a deliberate personal aesthetic.

paras: People wear it open over a tee, buttoned alone, or tucked with denim and boots. Fabrics are typically chambray, denim or tartan.
No health risks. Fit matters, and the strong Western association may read as costume in some settings.

angle.text: The yoke seams and snap detailing give the shirt a structured upper-body look and a recognizable retro-Western style.

lead: A Western shirt is a long-sleeved shirt with a stylized yoke front and back, usually made from chambray, denim or tartan; modern versions may add snap pockets or bandana patches.[1] Pearl snaps are the snap fasteners that replace buttons.

In 1946 Papa Jack Weil added snap buttons and pocket flaps to the Western shirt and founded Rockmount Ranch Wear in Denver.[1] Snap-front shirts were popularized by the singing cowboys of the 1940s and 1950s.[1] Young men embraced Western shirts in the 1960s and 1970s, and a 2012 GQ writer noted vintage washed-out Westerns from the 1970s becoming coveted.[1]

As an appearance tool, the yoke and snaps add visual structure and a vintage, outdoorsy identity. Research on clothing and perception exists in other contexts, for example a Saudi study of male physicians' outfits and patient perception, but no study tests this shirt.

paras: Defining features are the yoke on both front and back, long sleeves, and in many models snap closures and pocket flaps.[1]

The style draws on the Wild West era and on Mexican vaquero dress, with decorated versions worn by Roy Rogers and Clayton Moore in the 1950s.[1] Labels such as H Bar C and Panhandle Slim also made them.[1]
No studies found. A general study of clothing and perception, on physicians' outfits in Saudi Arabia, exists but does not cover this shirt.[2]
